quote: Yeah. I just saved a $219 power bill this month and $3,331 power bill last month.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers a bill figure unprompted in the opening seconds. Note the numbers here ($219 / $3,331) don't reconcile cleanly with the figures she gives later at 02:44 ($304, $506, roughly $1,000 across three-to-four months) — this is likely transcription/diarization noise on fast speech rather than two separate real bills, so the rep should not anchor hard on either specific figure without a bill-in-hand confirmation.
coaching_implication: Treat this as a signal of bill pain, not a reliable number to build a pitch on. The rep should have asked a clarifying follow-up ('just so I have it right, was that $219 or closer to $300?') rather than moving straight past it — flag the ambiguity in the moment instead of letting an unreconciled number sit uncorrected.

quote: So we have a program. It's called the bill swap. We look at your power bill, and we replace it with a lower and cheaper solar bill.
stewart_read: Rather than flipping the bill she just gave him into an emotional hook (their-bill-vs-ours framing), the rep explains the mechanism of the program generically. This is a missed flip opportunity right after she supplied a bill number.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have been trying to answer her direct 'what will this cost me' question first before circling back to the bill — a legitimate sequencing choice, but he never does circle back to tie the swap explicitly to her stated number.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to explicitly restate the customer's own number back to her inside the pitch ('so instead of that $219+ bill, you'd have a lower solar bill') rather than describing the program in the abstract.

quote: And then that's we have to lower your bill and save you money in the first year or we can't offer it. And then Say that again because I'm already hearing.
stewart_read: This line is garbled — likely audio crosstalk or the rep losing his own train of thought mid-pitch ('say that again because I'm already hearing' reads as the rep talking to himself about audio feedback). Whatever the cause, the delivery is unclear and undermines the legitimacy/confidence the program_pitch beat needs.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be a transcription artifact from Deepgram misattributing crosstalk rather than a genuine rep stumble — the audio itself would need review to confirm.
coaching_implication: Flag for audio review; if this is a real stumble it's a clarity/delivery coaching point — the program pitch is the customer's first real exposure to what Ion offers and should land cleanly.

quote: Just to remind you, I'm on Social Security. I don't get that much money, and my house payment's over $1,000 a month.
stewart_read: This is a fixed-income vulnerability disclosure, a trust gift per the schema. The rep's response is a flat administrative pivot straight into the address/homeowner verify question with no acknowledgment of what she just shared.
coaching_implication: Coach a specific acknowledgment move here — even one line ('I hear you, and that's exactly why this program exists for folks on a fixed budget') before continuing verify — rather than skipping straight past it.

quote: Because you have to have a credit score over 670 to qualify for the program.
stewart_read: The moment she reveals a sub-670 score, the rep states the hard rule and lets her self-disqualify with no alternative financing question, no probe into whether other programs exist, and no attempt to keep the lead warm for a future re-check.
alternative_hypothesis: If Ion's actual policy is hard-DQ-on-stated-credit with no alternative path, this is correct procedure and not a coaching gap — the schema itself flags this as an unresolved policy question (qualifiers.credit_qualifier.policy_question_for_kenny).
coaching_implication: Until the credit-DQ policy is clarified, coach the rep to at minimum anchor a concrete callback point ('credit scores can shift — let's check back in 90 days') instead of leaving it as a vague 'call you back' with no owned next step.

quote: I guess I just have to call you back whenever my credit goes up, my my credit score.
stewart_read: The call ends on a customer-initiated, vague callback promise with no date, no rep-owned follow-up, and no text/reminder plan — the opposite of the button-up protocol's handshake discipline.
coaching_implication: Even on a DQ, the rep should own the next step: 'Let's touch base in a few months — I'll reach back out then' or set a calendar reminder. Leaving it entirely on the customer to remember and re-initiate loses the lead.

quote: my thing is not right because I've got on here that I've been delinquent on two payments, and I haven't been delinquent on any payments for over two years.
stewart_read: Customer raises a specific, credible dispute about the accuracy of her own credit report (an erroneous delinquency mark and an unexplained 705-to-633 score drop) while checking her score live on the call. The rep never responds to this at all — it is not acknowledged before he moves straight to disqualifying her on the very numbers she just called into question.
coaching_implication: This is the strongest point in the call to have kept the lead alive — the customer is telling the rep her own bureau data may be wrong. A rep response like 'that's worth disputing with the bureau — let's still get you scheduled and the specialist can revisit this' would preserve the appointment instead of taking a disputed number as final.
